title: Jason Blum on How ‘Other Mommy’ Got That Controversial Title, Kristen Bell Joins ‘Violent Night 2’ and More From Blumhouse at NYCC
description: Jason Blum and James Wan aren’t paying much attention to the bad reviews (but massive box office success!) for “Other Mommy.” Instead, the horror ma
body:
Jason Blum and James Wan aren’t paying much attention to the bad reviews (but massive box office success!) for “Other Mommy.” Instead, the horror maestros spent Friday night looking ahead at what’s next, unveiling Blumhouse Atomic Monster’s upcoming slate of films during the 90-minute presentation at New York Comic-Con.

	In the next year, the horror house will launch a new installment of the “Exorcist” franchise starring Scarlett Johansson, “Violent Night 2” with Kristen Bell, new collaborations with MatPat and a revamped “Blair Witch Project.”
	

	If you couldn’t make it to the horror-filled presentation, read below for the major takeaways from the Blumhouse panel at NYCC.


	Jason Blum Addresses the Doppelganger Elephant In The Room

	Despite its major box office success, “Other Mommy” debuted this weekend to an onslaught of negative reviews. One of the things that was picked apart online was the title of the film itself, particularly why it wasn’t named “Other Mother” both for the sake of the rhyme and to further the parallels between “Coraline.”

	“Well, funnily enough, my partner James Wan wanted to call it ‘Other Mother,’ and he got outvoted,” Blum revealed during the panel. “This is probably why we should always listen to James Wan.”

	Kristen Bell Joins ‘Violent Night 2’ As Mrs. Clause

	Kristen Bell is getting into the Christmas spirit, and no, it isn’t with “Frozen.”

	The actress is joining David Harbour in “Violent Night 2,” stepping into the jolly-but-deadly shoes of Mrs. Clause. 
	

	“It was thrilling to get this call from David. I think I was so confused when he called, because I didn’t even know the were making a second one,” Bell said during the panel. “David called and said, ‘I need you to come to Winnipeg.’ And I was like, ‘What? No.'”

	As a big fan of the first film, Bell shared that once she learned it was for “Violent Night 2,” she was in. She revealed David told her she would play Mrs. Clause, who is a “‘badass, and she’s every bit as capable as Santa is.’ And I said, ‘Say more.’ And we made it work.”

	‘Paranormal Activity,’ ‘Blair Witch’ and ‘Saw 11’ Teased

	The fan-favorite film “Paranormal Activity” is getting a modern makeover and is set to release in theaters May 21, coming alongside the news of the Broadway play’s extension into February. 

	“‘Parnaormal Activity’ is such an emotional movie for me, because it’s really how Blumhouse started,” Blum shared. “It really gave birth to everything that we’ve done.”

	Wan and Blum announced the news with a teaser video of director Ian Tuason reenacting the infamous at-home footage of becoming posessed while sleeping overnight before turning to the camera to share the film is currently in production. 

	Craig Zobel Is Directing Adaptation of Comic Book Horror ‘Something Is Killing The Children’

	Director Craig Zobel announced he will direct the adaptation of James Tynion IV and Werther Dell’Edera’s “Something is Killing the Children.”

	Blumhouse is developing the franchise both as a live-action film and an adult animated television series, with Tynion IV spearheading the latter. Stephen Christy and James Tynion IV will produce the film for BOOM! Studios and Penguin Random House, alongside Jason Blum for Blumhouse. Shaun Sutton, Ryan Turek, Adam Yoelin and Mette Norkjaer will executive produce. Dell’Edera will as co-produce.

	Blumhouse Is Making More Than Just Movies

	The production company’s horror game, “Grave Seasons” is officially launching March 9, following years of teasing the game’s arrival. Blum shared they will also share prize packs that include Fortnite codes that celebrate the Purge’s Lady Liberty as part of Fortnightmares.

schema.headline: Jason Blum on How ‘Other Mommy’ Got That Controversial Title, Kristen Bell Joins ‘Violent Night 2’ and More From Blumhouse at NYCC

title: ‘Triangle of Sadness’ Producer Backs Park Syeyoung’s Memory-Bending Love Motel Drama ‘Satellite of Love’ at Busan Asian Project Market
description: A woman who has spent a decade shut inside a room at a rural love motel, waiting for the man who left her, discovers that the motel has been staging
body:
A woman who has spent a decade shut inside a room at a rural love motel, waiting for the man who left her, discovers that the motel has been staging her love life all along in “Satellite of Love,” the fourth feature from South Korean filmmaker Park Syeyoung (“The Fin”). 

	The project is part of the Asian Project Market, which runs within the Busan International Film Festival’s Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM).


	The motel sits among reed beds and woods, its rooms echoing with lovers every night. When her lover walks out, the woman insists he come back in 10 years, to the day and the hour. He says no. She stays put regardless, never leaving the room and cycling through the same chores – eating, washing up, laundering the sheets – while guests check in and out around her.
	

	A decade on, a man turns up saying he is the one who left. She doesn’t know his face, but he keeps at it, and slowly they fall in love. Then the cracks show. Their conversations start to loop. When he pleads with her to run away with him, the motel’s managers take him away.

	The truth is that the motel exists to keep the woman’s feelings alive and replay them. Men brought in from outside are coached to act out romances with her again and again, performing love, regret and guilt while their tears are gathered. Once she knows this, she goes back to her routine and turns her eyes to the door, waiting again for someone to come back.

	“I hope to convey the way in which our memories are so volatile and how the present can keep altering what has happened in the past,” Park says. “How nothing is definite and every memory is subject to change.”
	

	Park has been working on his third feature, “Who Stole My Cross?,” which is now in post-production. His first two features followed groups of characters from the outside, without digging into their inner wants, while “Who Stole My Cross?” centers on a single figure. That shift pushed him further, and he wants “Satellite of Love” to be driven entirely by its character. The script is in development.

	The film is produced by Coproduction Office’s Philippe Bober and creative producer Sylvain Cruiziat. The company has worked with Park on “The Masked Monster” and “The Fin,” which played Locarno in 2024 and 2025, respectively, and on “Who Stole My Cross?” Bober, who founded the company, produced Ruben Östlund’s Palme d’Or winners “Triangle of Sadness” and “The Square.” 

	The producers rank Park as a singular voice in present-day Korean cinema. “Satellite of Love” will be their fourth film together. “We are thrilled to continue supporting Syeyoung on his path as an auteur, and to accompany him on this next chapter,” they say.

	At the APM, the team wants to meet potential Asian co-production partners and financiers and to put Park’s next film in front of the industry early.

	Beyond “Satellite of Love,” Park is writing several commercial features he hopes to shoot in Korea alongside more personal projects he will make independently. “I will make films till I die, and I want to explore a range of financing approaches along the way,” he says.

schema.headline: ‘Triangle of Sadness’ Producer Backs Park Syeyoung’s Memory-Bending Love Motel Drama ‘Satellite of Love’ at Busan Asian Project Market

title: ‘Below’ Creator Breaks Down the Finale’s Last Shot, Josh Hartnett’s Accent and Season 2 Clues
description:
Oct 9, 2026 4:00pm PT	
	

	
	‘Below’ Creator Breaks Down the Finale’s Last Shot, Josh Hartnett’s Accent and Season 2 Clues
body:
Oct 9, 2026 4:00pm PT	
	

	
	‘Below’ Creator Breaks Down the Finale’s Last Shot, Josh Hartnett’s Accent and Season 2 Clues
	



			
			
	
						

									©Netflix/Courtesy Everett Collection
	
					


							
		

	SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for the first season of “Below,” now streaming on Netflix.

	Netflix’s new mystery series “Below” has arrived, and audiences are being transported to the beautiful and dangerous Newfoundland town of Snook’s Arm. Josh Hartnett stars as fisherman Calvin Penney, who, alongside Dr. Fonda Howander (Mackenzie Davis), is investigating a local mystery involving dirty ice and a giant sea monster. Calvin, Dr. Fonda, and his family get into plenty of adventures along the way, before an ending that promises a fresh start for the residents of Snook’s Arm … before a final moment that teases fresh danger, as several more icebergs approach, promising more deep-sea beasts on their way to Snook’s Arm.

	Variety spoke with “Below” creator and showrunner Jesse McKeown and executive producer Jessica Rhoades about Season 1’s ending, how the cast tackled the Newfoundland accent, the giant squid’s development and what might be explored in a second season.

	
		Where did the initial idea for “Below” come from?	

	Jesse McKeown: I’ve been going to Newfoundland for many, many years, and I had just always had a dream of making something there — something that was really big. There are a lot of smaller things that have been made in Newfoundland. There’s a strong film and television community there, but it’s very small. I wanted to do something that took advantage of the drama of the place. I never thought that would happen, but then, in a meeting with Netflix, an opportunity opened up and I snagged it and pitched them this and they went for it.



	

									Courtesy of Jan Thijs/Netflix
	





	
		How did you decide that you wanted Josh Hartnett and to have a strong Newfoundland accent?	

	Jessica Rhoades: I mean, you had to. I’d like to say it was some brilliant, bold move, but you have to get it right. Jesse has family in Newfoundland. He wasn’t going to be allowed to go home if we got it wrong. So the stakes are high. But both Josh — and Charlie [Heaton], and a few of the other actors like Ruby [Stokes] out of the U.K. — had done accent work. So they dove in.

	I think the hardest thing was finding an accent for the family. You wanted to sync them, as with any region. If you travel a bit, and depending on how long people have been there and what village, you hear the texture and difference in the accent. But for us it was about finding what the Penney family accent would be and how that could be a little different with the kids having gone away. How did we layer that on top of itself? That was the tricky bit, but Josh threw himself in from the day he said yes. He was studying and working.



	McKeown: My wife, who’s from Newfoundland, has three different accents. She has her generic North American accent. She has her townie, big-city St. John’s accent. And then she has her Bay accent. When she gets out into the rural-enough area, it gets even more pronounced. We really use that with the kids as modulating how long they’ve been on the mainland and how much they turn it up when they come home.

	I’ll just say Josh was incredible. Before he even came, he started listening to Newfoundland radio, the call-in shows and talk radio, which are like hugely popular in Newfoundland. There’s this show called “The Fisheries Broadcast,” which is the longest-running radio show in Canadian history. People just call in and talk about the fishery, and so he just immersed himself in that. He already had it in his head before he set foot on the island.

	Rhoades: We’re also happy that we knew, making it for Netflix, I watch my kids and my parents watch with subtitles on. We knew a majority of the audience might be watching that way anyway, and that gave us the ability to be really true to the accent.

	McKeown: I love shows like “The Wire” where I may not understand every little thing, but I know it means something to the character and then I’ll find out what it means. I like to give the audience something to dig into.


	
		Did you always envision this season to be six relatively short episodes?	

	McKeown: We always wanted to treat it like an event, and that’s what Netflix wanted as well. We were totally aligned on that, which is rare because limited series are kind of hard to get made. I was really excited about that. We approached it as, “OK, we have six episodes to tell a complete and satisfying story.” That’s what we tried to do.



	

									Courtesy of Jan Thijs/Netflix
	




	
		How did you decide what level of flirtation Calvin and Dr. Fonda would have this season? Were they ever going to hook up?	

	Rhoades: It’s interesting. It wasn’t in Jesse’s pitch. We cast Josh and Mackenzie and we all decided it was more about these two coming out of their shells and being able to communicate with someone, and coming out of isolation and we were playing with so many of those themes. And then the two of them just up and had some chemistry, and we had to contend with it. There’s a moment obviously in the end where I dare you to not be rooting for them, but it just happened. You just want those two kids together, don’t you?

	McKeown: I feel like it sort occurred to both of them at the same time in that moment. “OK, finally we’ve dealt with everything for now.” On the page, it was more important that, “OK, he’s taking a step toward the community and so has she. They’re both two lonely people that have opened up a little bit, and they’ve become part of each other’s lives.” But it was there on the day.


	
		Without jumping the gun, have you dreamed up a lot of ideas for a potential second season?	

	McKeown: Not in any serious way. Obviously there are things that you think about during the course of making it, little pipe dreams and offshoots. And we never wanted to wrap up the ending in a tidy little bow anyway. But no, I haven’t thought about it at all.


	
		The sea hag visions: we get an explanation for it in the show, but is there more than meets the eye there?	

	McKeown: It was from personal experience. I’ve had sleep paralysis. I didn’t know it was called the old hag, but I used to get it quite a bit when I was younger, more as a teenager and in my 20s. I think it was stress-related or something, but I had a version of a this female creature in my room who would watch me sleep and climb and then I found out it was a thing. Then I found out that’s a mythology that crosses cultures. You’ll find versions of that mythology all over the world. For some reason, it’s very popular in Newfoundland. Everyone talks about the hag: “Oh yeah, I had the hag last night. She came to me.” It’s just part of the vernacular, so I wanted to build on it. I do think it is Wade is under stress and he’s got all these problems. So it’s very plausible that it was something psychological, but then it turns out not to be.



	

									Courtesy of Netflix
	




	
		How did you come up with the look of the giant squid?	

	McKeown: There was a lot of research that we did ahead of time. We talked to some experts. One was sort of like a real-life Fonda. Her name is Dr. Annie Mercier, and she works at that actual building, the Ocean Sciences Centre, which is a real place in Newfoundland. We’d talk to her just about cephalopods and how they behave. There’s a long and rich history of Architeuthis dux, the North Atlantic giant squid, in that area of Newfoundland. That’s where all the original discoveries happened. So the giant squid is very important to the history and mythology of Newfoundland. Once you open your eyes for that, you’ll see it everywhere. There’s statues of the giant squid, there’s museums dedicated to it, you see it everywhere. So it really had to be that creature for Newfoundland. But we wanted it to be more than just the North Atlantic giant squid. We want it to be something even more unknown and something more mysterious. So we talked to experts about what would plausibly be a previously undetected ancestor of the giant squid that we know, and then so we worked backward and extrapolated from that.

	Rhoades: There is so much time modeling and doing scales and being able to figure out boats, houses, ships, all of those things. It was a really complex multiteam. Obviously, it was our VFX team, but it was also an SFX team. It’s everyone working with production design. Everything had to be so precise to get the scale of her right. You don’t want it to be silly, obviously, but you want it to be fun, but it had to be scary. I think one of our biggest challenges was like the scope of the eye outside of the submersible, just getting those things right.


	
		Episode 5 is very dreamlike. Did you always know you wanted to have an episode that broke form and gave a different vibe than the rest of the series?	

	McKeown: Totally. That was really what we wanted to do with that episode. I love when shows end up taking you to a place that you never thought you would go to, you could never see coming. But it was also like a really important step on Calvin’s journey. He says at the very beginning, “I’m not moving an inch, I’m never leaving this place.” It’s very important for him to go through that and understand, “This is what it might look like if you don’t leave. If everybody packs up and leaves and you decide to stick it out without the community, and without the people that make these outports viable, this is the dark side of your dream and your vision.” There’s no easy answers. I think Calvin and his family and people like that are in a very difficult position. And Walton [Shawn Doyle] and his family decided to stick it out as best they could. I think there’s something really appealing about that. That’s why I love that episode so much, because Calvin buys into the dream a little bit before it turns completely nightmarish.



	

									Courtesy of Jan Thijs/Netflix
	




	
		Shooting on location makes the series feel so much more dynamic and real. But what were some of the complications in doing that?	

	Rhoades: Simultaneously, you don’t want people thinking too much about how hard it must have been to shoot. You want people just to be able to enjoy and stay in it. But it’s nice that people feel it, because it was really hard. It was a really tangible show. We wanted it to feel as real as possible. Newfoundland made that easy because you could just do it. We were on open water. We were out on the island.

	McKeown: Newfoundland is a hard place to exist even when you’re not making a giant TV show on the water. It likes to throw a lot of curveballs at you on a good day, and it’s a dangerous place. But I think that comes through on the screen, and we had an amazing team and a crew that is used to working near the water, so that was indispensable. But there was no question about us shooting there, it had to be that way.


	
		Did you always know that last shot with the icebergs was going to be the ending?	

	McKeown: I feel like you always try everything on for size as you’re going, but the idea of that visual was there from the very beginning, in the outline for the show. I think in some ways it is a happy ending for Calvin and his family, but it’s a reprieve. They get to live to fight another day, and so it was important not to turn away from the real catastrophe that’s heading for us.

	Rhoades: I think it’s so beautifully built with what Jesse built in the first episode. Calvin’s looking out for himself and his family, and says “When those icebergs come rolling in, you know who to call.” She obviously is ahead of him in this tale, and what those mean, to be able to take it all the way to its ending. It just felt perfect.


	
		The series ultimately mirrors the journey of a human family with that of a giant squid family. Was that something you thought about from the beginning, or a connection that came later?	

	McKeown: It came in the process. Cephalopods and those deep-sea creatures are so lonely to me, and they’re so incredible and fascinating. The more you learn about them, the more you can’t help but personify them a little bit. The fact that they mate once and give birth to these giant blobs filled with thousands and thousands of eggs and then, maybe, two or three of them will survive. And then they pass away, in the process of sitting with their brood and giving them life, they die. So that just really struck me. I feel like Calvin has a different relationship to it at the beginning, a different relationship to nature and to his environment, a different relationship to the icebergs. But after everything he goes through and he learns the truth, he learns a different way of relating to his environment that felt really right to make that connection between them. For him to have kind of one of those cosmic moments that I have sometimes, one of those moments where you suddenly feel that connection to everything around you.


	
		Is the baby creature in the lab still alive, roaming around? 	

	[Rhoades and McKeown smile and give big shoulder shrugs, indicating they couldn’t possibly know the answer to that.]



	

									Courtesy of Netflix
	




	
		Is Calvin’s sister Ruth (Willow Kean) in a throuple with the two people she lives with?	

	McKeown: I’m happy to answer that: Yes, Ruth is in a throuple.

	Rhoades: Obviously, there are big stories to tell. There’s a lot of stories. Jesse built so many different characters and so much texture to the town. You can only foreground as much of it as we can. So it’s there, and we’re so happy it’s there.

	McKeown: There’s a lot of wild stuff happening around the bay, I’ll tell you that much. They’re open-minded, adventurous people.

	This interview has been edited and condensed.

schema.headline: ‘Below’ Creator Breaks Down the Finale’s Last Shot, Josh Hartnett’s Accent and Season 2 Clues

title: ‘Other Mommy’: Five Biggest Changes From the Book, Including a Crazy Death Scene and a Much Darker Ending
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains major spoilers from “Other Mommy,” now playing in theaters.

	“Other Mommy” is battling less-than-enthusiastic re
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains major spoilers from “Other Mommy,” now playing in theaters.

	“Other Mommy” is battling less-than-enthusiastic reviews in order to lead the weekend box office, thanks to a viral trailer that scared audiences nationwide.

	The film, about a sinister demon who befriends a little girl named Bela (Arabella Olivia Clark) and takes the appearance of her mother Ursula (Jessica Chastain), is based on Josh Malerman’s 2024 novel “Incidents Around the House.” The book, of course, goes much more in depth into Bela’s story, but the film takes plenty of other liberties in bringing the tale to the big screen.
	

	Below, Variety has gathered the five biggest differences between the book and the film, from one jaw-dropping scene the movie adds to the much darker ending of the book.
	
		The look of the demon	

	In “Other Mommy,” the demon is skilled at mimicking humans during the whole runtime. There are moments where, as Other Mommy, it has specific tells, like face drooping or levitation slightly off the floor. But largely it’s a convincing mimic.

	There are more signs of something nefarious in the book, as the demon is more avian in appearance, has less steady facial features, carries a putrid smell and an essence that causes some people to cough.
	
		A deadly séance	

	One of the key scenes of the film is a séance set up by Grandma Ruth (Karen Allen), which ends with a well-equipped but naive ghost hunting squad conjuring Other Mommy, and getting unceremoniously killed for their troubles.

	In the book, a séance is set up by fake spiritualists, who quickly admit that they can’t help and are in over their heads.
	
	
		A change of scenery	

	One of the most memorable setpieces in “Other Mommy” takes place at a Chuck E. Cheese-esque restaurant, where Bela follows who she thinks is a new friend. But, of course, it’s the demon, and Bela is pulled into an endless ball pit as her father Russell (Jay Duplass) and Ursula dive in to find her. Bela is then transported to the sea, and then the family sedan, which is now filled up with the ball pit balls — as well as Other Mommy. 

	It’s a more visually dynamic version of a tense, equivalent scene early in the novel, which takes place at a playground and ends with Bela taking a big fall. But what works on the page is made more arresting for the silver screen and creates a trailer-ready moment.
	
		A gory added scene	

	The film’s wildest horror moment is when family friend Frank (Arian Moayed) invites Russell, Ursula and Bela to stay at his fancy mansion after Other Mommy disrupts the couple’s anniversary party. Although they are searching for safety, Bela can sense family tension around Frank, as he is a friend of Russell who is not-so-secretly having an affair with Ursula. 

	While Bela is using the bathroom, Other Mommy approaches her and tricks her into agreeing that their family would be better if Frank wasn’t around. This inspires Other Mommy to gruesomely kill Frank in front of Bela, including blowing his head up in an outrageous explosion of blood.

	In the book, Ursula simply announces that Frank was found dead in a closet, which is a far less traumatic moment for Bela.
	
		That ending	

	In the film, Bela refuses to let Other Mommy into her heart, per the demon’s constant request. This eventually defeats Other Mommy, leaving the happy family of three intact — even though there’s subtext that Bela will always have a little discomfort around her mother.

	In the exceedingly bleak ending to the book, Bela realizes that the demon has killed and styled itself after her Grandma Ruth, who lures Russell and Ursula to their death. Fully alone, Bela agrees to let Other Mommy into her heart, which effectively means that Other Mommy takes over Bela’s body, and Bela is left in the purgatory that the demon had come from. It’s dark!

	Watch the “Other Mommy” trailer below.

schema.headline: ‘Other Mommy’: Five Biggest Changes From the Book, Including a Crazy Death Scene and a Much Darker Ending

title: ‘The Exorcist: Martyrs’ Trailer Unveiled at NYCC: Scarlett Johansson Stars in Horror Sequel From Mike Flanagan
description:

	Chiwetel Ejiofor and director, writer and producer Mike Flanagan unveiled the trailer for “The E
body:
“The Exorcist” franchise is about to get bigger. 

	Chiwetel Ejiofor and director, writer and producer Mike Flanagan unveiled the trailer for “The Exorcist: Martyrs” at New York City Comic Con, with Scarlett Johansson starring as a homicide detective who soon realizes she isn’t dealing with a normal serial killer. 

	Releasing in theaters March 12, the trailer shows a slew of gruesome murders that were committed in a church, prompting Johansson’s character to question if the claims of previous killers alleging they were posessed by Satan could, in fact, have merit.
	

	Starring alongside Ejiofor and Johansson are John Leguizamo, Laurence Fishburne, Diane Lane and “Hamnet” star Jacobi Jupe. 


	Prior to revealing the trailer, Flanagan teased “The Exorcist: Martyrs” is the scariest project he’s done in his career. 

	“This movie is unlike any other ‘Exorcist’ movie that’s ever been made, which was something that we were really determined to do from the very beginning,  to take this franchise in a completely different direction,” Flanagan said during the panel. “And one of the things that we all kind of agreed on going in was that it had to be scary. It had to just be goddamn scary, like to your bones scary.”

	Universal bought the rights for a new “Exorcist” trilogy for $400 million in 2021, launching with “The Excorcist: Believer” two years later. However, Flanagan’s film will not serve as a sequel to the 2023 movie.

	“’The Exorcist’ is one of the reasons I became a filmmaker, and it is an honor to have the chance to try something fresh, bold and terrifying within its universe,” Flanagan said in 2024. “Reuniting with my friends at Blumhouse, with whom I’ve made some of my favorite pieces of work, only makes this more exciting.”
	

	This is Flanagan’s fourth collaboration with Blumhouse, previously writing and directing 2013’s “Oculus,” 2016’s “Hush” and 2016’s “Ouija: Origin of Evil.” The three films were produced by Trevor Macy, who will return as producer for “The Exorcist: Martyrs” on behalf of Intrepid Pictures.

	Alexandra Magistro executive produces for Red Room Pictures alongside Topher Merrill and John Baden executive produce for Morgan Creek Entertainment. Trevor Macy, Karl Frankenfield, David Robinson and Roy Lee produce, and Jason Blum and Ryan Turek serve as producer and executive producer for Blumhouse-Atomic Monster.

	“The Exorcist: Martyrs” is a Blumhouse-Atomic Monster and Morgan Creek Entertainment production, in association with Flanagan’s Red Room Pictures. The film was originally set to premiere this March but was pushed to 2027 after production was delayed.

	The original “The Exorcist” released in 1973 and was directed by William Friedkin, following a mother (Ellen Burstyn) who hired Catholic priests to perform an exorcism on her 12-year-old daughter (Linda Blair) who became possessed by a demon. The film went on to earn $441 million globally and received 10 Oscar nominations.

	Watch the trailer below.

schema.headline: ‘The Exorcist: Martyrs’ Trailer Unveiled at NYCC: Scarlett Johansson Stars in Horror Sequel From Mike Flanagan

title: Blumhouse Atomic Monster Inks Short Film Development Deal with Horror Creator Heidi Wong
description: Blumhouse Atomic Monster revealed at New York Comic Con that it inked a deal with horror content creator Heidi Wong. Under the deal, Wong will creat
body:
Blumhouse Atomic Monster revealed at New York Comic Con that it inked a deal with horror content creator Heidi Wong. Under the deal, Wong will create original horror shorts for the studio. 

	“I guess I won’t give too much away about the plot, but I will say it’s inspired by Eastern mythology and folklore and I grew up in Asia, so it’s very close to me,” Wong said when announcing the project alongside Jason Blum at the Blumfest panel at New York Comic Con Friday. “And to have Blumhouse’s support really means so, so much.”
	

	Wong, who was featured on Time’s 2025 100 Creators List and Forbes 30 Under 30, is best known for telling and reenacting stories on social media based on horror movies. She also shares recommendations and ratings for films in the genre. Wong’s love of horror goes back to her childhood, when she taught herself English by reading scary stories. 


	Wong, known as “The Horror Queen” to her fans, has a global fanbase of over 8 million followers. She’s helped create content for Netflix, Sony, 20th Century Studios, Paramount Pictures, Universal and AMC. Before she posted her first storytelling TikTok in 2020, Wong earned six consecutive national art competition wins and received nominations for the Pushcart Prize and Dylan Thomas Prize for her poetry collection “Turning to Wallpaper.” Wong recently completed her Master of Fine Arts in Poetry from New York University.

	Blumhouse Atomic Monster is one of the most productive horror studios in Hollywood. It was behind two of the biggest genre hits of 2026: “Obsession” and “The Backrooms.” This year, Blumhouse released “SoulM8ate,” “The Uprising,” “Five Nights at Freddy’s 2,” “Lee Cronin’s The Mummy,” “Insidious: Out of the Further,” and most recently, “Other Mommy.” Upcoming releases from the studio include “Play House,” Curry Barker’s “Anything But Ghosts,” “The Exorcist: Martyrs,” a “Paranormal Activity” sequel and a “Blair Witch Project” reboot.

title: An AI-Generated Trailer Won the Inaugural $2.5 Million Future Vision XPRIZE — and Its Director Hopes It’ll Change Minds About AI
description: Director Jeff T. Thomas has worked on dozens of television episodes and music videos, some featuring the likes of Arnold Schwarzenegger and Melissa
body:
Director Jeff T. Thomas has worked on dozens of television episodes and music videos, some featuring the likes of Arnold Schwarzenegger and Melissa Leo. But with AI, his feature debut is nigh.

	Thomas, under his moniker “Jeff Synthesized,” took home the $2.5 million “Future Vision XPRIZE” last month with the AI-generated proof-of-concept trailer for “The Gifted.” (Watch the trailer below.) The trailer was made with the prompt of depicting “a future worth building toward” within three minutes. The competition was judged by astrophysicist Neil deGrasse Tyson, novelist Neal Stephenson, Google‘s Mira Lane, Salesforce executive John Zissimos and ‘Star Trek’ steward Rod Roddenberry. Thomas’ trailer follows an 11-year-old boy who builds an AI version of his late mother who rebuilds his late mother that quietly begins saving lives, captured through various moments.
	

	Now, with the win, Google and Range Media Partners (through their 100 Zeroes initiative) will help develop the trailer into a full-length feature.


	It’s a story partly inspired by Thomas’ own childhood, having lost his mother at 14 due to an undiagnosed brain tumor. But having to navigate designing a hopeful film, one devoid of an antagonist that also heralds a positive view of AI, was a challenge in its own right. 

	But Thomas hopes the project can be a vehicle for that positive view of AI, both narratively and as a production tool, even as many in Hollywood remain fearful about its impact on jobs and some in the general public worry about its world-ending potential.

	“I wanted to follow a character that became obsessive, compulsive about trying to bring his mother back,” he tells Variety. “In the movie that we’ll see, she admits to not being his actual mother, but she does actually end up helping him, helping the world, and hopefully this will be something that will be imitated by technology people, and we can actually do some good in the world.”
	

	The participants — roughly 2,500, with the top five making it in front of the judges — were not required to use AI, but the fact that many of the final submissions was “evidence that AI is preoccupying people’s thoughts,” Tyson tells Variety.

	Tyson says he found the trailer a “clever construct” in how it flipped people’s general fears about the technology’s “all-knowing” nature into a tool that connects people to help each other. His fellow judges agreed. “The choice of the number one was unanimous,” he says.

	But that doesn’t mean he’s eager for completely AI-generated films, saying people flock to movies because “we want to see what humans can do” and that audiences will demand “human creativity, not machine creativity.”

	“[AI] will raise the bar on creativity,” he says. “You can’t just be an artist aping the work of other artists because AI can do that. The value of that will drop in the workplace, but something that’s truly creative that comes out of the deepest parts of the minds of someone who dreamt it — I don’t see AI coming for that anytime soon.”

	For Roddenberry, he says he wanted to see a project that could be “the next ‘Star Trek,’” one that left audiences believing the world the three-minute trailer presents is one they could aspire to.

	“Is [the story] believable? No,” he admits. “It’s make believe. It can’t connect it exactly to reality, but I think it’s just a beautiful story of how technology, especially something like AI, which is so feared today, can have a positive message in it.”

	It’s a philosphy Range subscribes to, CEO Peter Micelli says, investing in the prize to both showcase how people are using AI tools within the film industry and source new stories from contestants across the world. While the eventual “roughly $10 million” film will not be AI generated, he says, it’s a technology that could mimic the look of a film that costs 10 times that figure.

	“This reality is here,” Micelli says. “This tool is very, very powerful. And I would be more concerned about us not being involved in these things because we need to be on the ground floor so we can advise our clients and partners that are established in Hollywood on [how] this is a reality, and everyone needs to be aware of what it is.”
	

	Not that Thomas plans on making an AI film, promising his eventual movie will only utilize it as a tool. But he also doesn’t want those in the industry to write off AI as an end-all killer of creativity, pointing to his use of it while directing episodes of  Amazon’s “House of David” series and his own experimentation with AI models.

	“Audiences are still expecting $25 million-looking episodes, but you might have $10 million, you might have $12 million,” he says. “What AI can do is fill in the gaps between those to still provide the audience with something they want and still allow the studios to make the material for what they can afford. So, creatively wise, I think it will make entertainment better, because you won’t be as limited as we have been up until this point.”

	Watch the trailer here:

title: AI Grief-Bot Dramedy ‘Talk to Me When You Are Dead,’ Produced by Anthony Chen, Probes the Limits of Digital Afterlives at Busan Asian Project Market
description: A widowed programmer who builds a digital copy of his late wife ends up turning grief into a business in “Talk to Me When You Are Dead,” the debut f
body:
A widowed programmer who builds a digital copy of his late wife ends up turning grief into a business in “Talk to Me When You Are Dead,” the debut feature from Singapore’s Alvin Lee, produced by Anthony Chen and Gina Tan. 

	The project is part of the Asian Project Market, which runs within the Busan International Film Festival’s Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM).

	In the near-future story, Yong Yi makes a digital replica of his wife Kate to cope with losing her. A friend spots a market and talks him into a startup that sells grief-bots to the newly bereaved. Yong Yi is then hired to quietly build a replica of Mr. Yun, a celebrated architect who is terminally ill. Hiding his real purpose to get close to him, Yong Yi records Mr. Yun’s memories, and the two grow into something like father and son. As Mr. Yun weakens, Yong Yi must choose between finishing a well-paid job and protecting a fragile man he now cares about, a crisis that finally makes him face what really happened to Kate. The project is pitched as a black dramedy that probes the line between real connection and digital preservation.
	

	Lee began the film while grieving his best friend, who died four years ago. While he was writing, a relative asked him to create an AI-generated video of someone the family had lost. “I made it, and it gave real comfort to people I love, and I still do not know what to think about that,” Lee says. “The person in it was not really him, but the comfort it created was real. That contradiction became the starting point of the film.”


	Lee says he hopes audiences leave with a sense of hope and a reminder to hold on to their humanity as technology floods everyday life. “We can also live in comfort and denial, but many times the pain that breaks us is part of us, and vital to our growth. That is what makes us human,” he says.
	

	After several years in development, the script is now in its third draft.

	Chen, who has tracked Lee’s short films since Lee was in film school, worked with him on shaping his first feature. “It has taken a few reiterations before we landed on this idea and I’m heartened that it comes from a personal place yet has wide universal appeal,” Chen says.

	Tan, who met Lee five years ago on joining one of his shorts, praises the light touch he brings to a range of subjects. “He does not flinch from the hard things, but he never lets them become heavy-handed. That sensibility is precisely what ‘Talk to Me When You Are Dead’ demands, and precisely why he is the right person to make it,” Tan says.

	Busan marks the project’s first outing, and the producers want it to put Lee on the map as a first-time feature director. They also hope to find co-producers, financiers and other collaborators, and believe the story is universal enough to travel across regions.

	Lee is also developing his next idea, which takes on present-day Singapore concerns, among them a low birth rate and a shortage of land, and adds a supernatural element.

schema.headline: AI Grief-Bot Dramedy ‘Talk to Me When You Are Dead,’ Produced by Anthony Chen, Probes the Limits of Digital Afterlives at Busan Asian Project Market

title: Adéla Brings Sass, Vocals and Razor-Sharp Moves to Los Angeles’ Fonda Theatre
description: Amid the first of two sold-out nights at Los Angeles’ Fonda Theatre on Thursday night, Adéla paused to shout out Katseye members Lara Raj and Megan
body:
Amid the first of two sold-out nights at Los Angeles’ Fonda Theatre on Thursday night, Adéla paused to shout out Katseye members Lara Raj and Megan Skindiel, who were watching in the balcony alongside Saint Satine’s Emily Kelavos. “I moved out here a couple of years ago; I moved here for the show that I was on,” said Adéla, referring to Netflix’s “Pop Star Academy,” a competition to join the group that would become Katseye. (Spoiler: she didn’t make it past the first round.) “It’s crazy because my best friends that I met through the show are here tonight. We would train just down the street every day for two years and try to become pop stars together. And guess what, that didn’t work out for me but it did for them, shout out to y’all.”
	

	That clearly isn’t true, as Adéla has spent the past year charting a path towards becoming one of pop’s most promising new stars. Though she’s been steadily grinding for years, she only recently hit full throttle following the release of her debut album “Prima” last month, spawning not one but two simultaneous hits, the swaggery “Nicole Kidman” and “Ain’t in LA.” On Spotify’s Global 50 chart, those songs are currently Nos. 2 and 4, respectively. Earlier this week, Kidman herself cashed in on her namesake song’s success, filming a TikTok along to the track with Kristen Wiig, Pedro Pascal and Dua Lipa.




	

					Adéla performs during The Red Bottoms Tour at The Fonda Theatre on October 08, 2026 in Los Angeles, California.
									Michael Buckner
	



	All of this, at least by the temperature inside the Fonda last night, felt well-earned. Adéla is a showwoman in the purest sense, working every angle and performing from her gut. As part of her headlining “Red Bottoms” tour, she traipsed through cuts from “Prima” and her debut EP “The Provocateur,” echoing the hallmarks of pop royalty — the razor-sharp dance moves of Britney, the sass of Madonna (whose classic “Vogue” was mashed with opening song “KGB,” perhaps not coincidentally), all with an unmistakable and signature look to match. (Fans throughout the venue wore shock-pink wigs in tribute.)
	



	

					Chappell Roan appears in the audience for Adéla’s The Red Bottoms Tour at The Fonda Theatre on October 08, 2026 in Los Angeles, California.
									Michael Buckner
	



	It came as no surprise, then, that those at the Fonda — including a gobsmacked Chappell Roan, who watched from the balcony — lapped up every bit of it. In knee-high pink heels, Adéla led a team of backup dancers on an empty stage accented by a dance barre, a nod to her own training as a ballet dancer. She went back to where it all began, with songs like “Superscar” and “DeathByDevotion,” while peppering in “Prima” cuts like “Red Bottoms and “I’m the Man.” 

	Adéla has made her intentions widely known: she wants to be a pop star. (She said as much on “KGB,” sneering, “I wanna pop off so these big mouths can’t say shit.”) Perhaps, if her Fonda show was any indication, that moment may have already arrived.



	

					Adéla performs during The Red Bottoms Tour at The Fonda Theatre on October 08, 2026 in Los Angeles, California.
									Michael Buckner

									Michael Buckner

title: LaKeith Stanfield Previews ‘Molepeople’ Movie From Paramount Primal, Blumhouse Atomic Monster at New York Comic-Con
description:
Oscar nominee LaKeith Stanfield previewed his next movie, “Molepeople,” during a special appearance at New York Comic-Con on Friday evening.

	Stanf
body:
Oscar nominee LaKeith Stanfield previewed his next movie, “Molepeople,” during a special appearance at New York Comic-Con on Friday evening.

	Stanfield and Emmy winner Ben Mendelsohn star in the horror movie, about a man who descends into the abandoned tunnels beneath New York City, where he discovers a “twisted society lurking beneath the streets.”

	The film — directed by Rob Savage from a script by Nathan Elston — will be co-financed and co-produced by Blumhouse Atomic Monster and Paramount Primal, with Paramount handling worldwide distribution. Onstage, Stanfield announced that “Molepeople” has been set for theatrical release on Aug. 27, 2027.  
	

	Producers include Blumhouse Atomic Monster chief Jason Blum; Paramount Primal heads J.D. Lifshitz and Raphael Margules; and James Harris. Elston and Savage are executive producers alongside Ryan Turek and Tracy Rosenblum.


	The project represents a merging between Paramount Primal — one of the key specialty labels in Skydance’s film division, specializing in “smartly budgeted” projects with a distinct point of view and “pulp sensibility” — and Blumhouse Atomic Monster — which spent two decades innovated that methodology of churning out low-budget horror hits.

	Paramount Primal’s upcoming slate includes “Boys for Life,” with Alex Wolff, set for theatrical release on April 9, 2027; “Sweet Spot,” a high-concept thriller spec from writing duo Nic Curcio and Kirby Gladstein; and “The Troop,” based on the acclaimed horror novel by Nick Cutter. The label also recently acquired the U.S. rights to adapt the original screenplay for “A Nightmare on Elm Street” from the Wes Craven estate, and is developing the R-rated fantasy “Tower Defense” from writer Evan Daugherty.
	

	In 2024, Blum’s Blumhouse merged with James Wan’s Atomic Monster; the combined company has grossed more than $10 billion in worldwide box office and has represented approximately half of the horror market over the last decade. 

	Blumhouse Atomic Monster has produced over 250 movies and television series, including the “Conjuring” universe, the most successful horror franchise in history; additional franchises include “Halloween,” “The Purge,” “The Black Phone,” “Annabelle,” “Paranormal Activity,” “The Exorcist,” “Insidious,” “The Nun,” “M3GAN” and “Five Nights at Freddy’s.” This year, “Obsession” and “Backrooms” became the highest-grossing films ever for Focus Features and A24, respectively, and helped Blumhouse Atomic Monster hit $1 billion in worldwide box office for the second year in a row. The company’s latest film “Other Mommy” is expected to top this week’s box office charts, despite negative reviews. 

	“Molepeople” marks Stanfield’s third movie with Blumhouse, following a bit part in 2014’s “The Purge: Anarchy” and a key role in Jordan Peele’s Oscar-winning 2017 film “Get Out.”

	More to come…

description:
Ella Langley
                          I'm Choosing Safety You Can Tell
body:
Ella Langley
                          I'm Choosing Safety You Can Tell
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 9, 2026
                            3:09 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  October 9, 2026
                                4:08 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Ella Langley won't be taking the stage in Oklahoma tonight ... her show's been canceled due to a "serious security threat."
      
    
            Tulsa's BOK Center took to social media to announce the abrupt cancellation, writing ... "Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of fans, venue personnel, and the artist, Ella Langley's scheduled performance tonight at BOK Center in Tulsa has been canceled."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The venue went on to say that safety was their top priority, and that's why they decided to pull the plug on the performance.
      

            They continued ... "We understand the disappointment this news brings and apologize to fans who planned to attend. The safety of fans is our foremost concern and will always come first."
      
    
            The venue didn't explicitly say what kind of threat they were facing, but said they'll provide additional information and details about refunds as soon as they can.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Ella also shared the venue's message, writing in her Instagram caption ... "This decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue, and my security team."
      
    
            She continued ... "I know how much time, travel, money, and planning goes into coming to a show, and I can’t tell you how sorry I am. This is not a decision that was made lightly."
      
    
            Ella concluded her caption by saying ... "I was so looking forward to spending tonight with you, but your safety will always mean more to me than anything else. I refuse to put anyone in harm's way."

            The judge in the case said Bell would be back in court for a plea and preparation hearing at the end of November.
      
    
            A provisional date for the trial has been set for the beginning of April 2027.

        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.

            Laura also argues it's either "disingenuous or misinformed" for Altman to claim that experts aren't sure what to do, writing ... "Researchers have been saying loud and clear: We need user data and chatbot interactions to conduct research."
      
    
            She says she would gladly hand over her late daughter Sophie's chat log if it meant it could help researchers determine "what pushes someone from vague suicidal ideation to executing on a suicide plan."
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            But when the potential solution was recently floated to Altman, he argued that it would be a violation of privacy to access someone's private chat logs.
